entities.summary:
Bulgarian stands as the oldest attested Slavic language, a cornerstone of South Slavic linguistic identity and a vital conduit for Orthodox Christian culture across Eastern Europe. Its written tradition commenced in the 9th century with the creation of the Glagolitic alphabet by Saints Cyril and Methodius, subsequently evolving into Cyrillic by their disciples, most notably Clement of Ohrid and Naum of Preslav. This linguistic innovation, often referred to as Old Church Slavonic in its earliest literary form, facilitated the Christianization and cultural development of numerous Slavic peoples, profoundly shaping the intellectual and spiritual landscape of the First Bulgarian Empire and beyond.

During the First Bulgarian Empire (681–1018), Old Bulgarian became the official language of state and church, flourishing particularly under Tsar Simeon I (r. 893–927), whose reign is considered the Golden Age of medieval Bulgarian culture. Preslav and Ohrid emerged as crucial literary centers where a vast corpus of religious texts, hagiographies, chronicles, and original theological works were translated from Greek or composed anew. This period saw the standardization of the Cyrillic script, which, crucially, offered a phonetic representation uniquely suited for Slavic phonology, unlike the Latin or Greek alphabets used by neighboring powers. The literary output not only served the needs of the Bulgarian state but also established a model for other emerging Slavic literatures.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Bulgarian, through its Old Bulgarian form, was instrumental in the creation and dissemination of the Cyrillic alphabet, which today serves hundreds of millions across Eastern Europe and Asia. It laid the linguistic and literary foundation for numerous other Slavic languages and cultures, profoundly shaping their religious, political, and intellectual development.
